stem: A nurse is inserting an indwelling urinary catheter in an acute-care hospital. Which technique is required?

options.A: Clean nonsterile technique with reusable lubricant
options.C: Sterile gloves only; the remaining insertion supplies may be nonsterile
options.D: No specific aseptic technique if the catheter will be removed within 24 hours

rationale: CDC CAUTI guidance states that in acute-care hospitals, urinary catheters should be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. Recommended supplies include sterile gloves, drape, sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet.
educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and sterile equipment when inserting an indwelling urinary catheter in acute care.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections — Summary of Recommendations
source_version_date: 2009 guideline with CDC updates; current summary accessed 2026
source_locator: Section II Proper Techniques for Urinary Catheter Insertion, Recommendations II.C and II.C.1
source_claim_supported: In acute-care hospitals, urinary catheters should be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment, including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate cleansing solution, and single-use lubricant.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
correction_summary: Clarified the care setting because CDC allows clean technique for chronic intermittent catheterization in some non-acute settings. Replaced the overly broad 'strict sterile technique throughout' wording with the exact CDC requirement: aseptic technique using sterile equipment.
audit_findings: B directly matches CDC II.C. A could apply to chronic intermittent catheterization outside acute care but not this stem; C and D are inconsistent with the sterile-equipment requirement. No second answer remains.
